reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / lacrimal disease literature
clinicalPearls: A chronic infection of the lacrimal canaliculus that is frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent conjunctivitis
Presents with a red, tender, pouting punctum, unilateral discharge and epiphora
Expression of the canaliculus may release characteristic concretions (sulphur-like granules)
The classic organism is Actinomyces israelii, though other bacteria and fungi occur
It is often unilateral and resistant to topical antibiotics alone
Definitive treatment usually requires removal of the concretions, commonly by canaliculotomy and curettage
reference.pathophysiology: Canaliculitis is infection within the lacrimal canaliculus, most classically by the filamentous bacterium Actinomyces israelii, which forms concretions (dacryoliths) within the lumen. These concretions harbour organisms and perpetuate the infection, causing chronic inflammation, a pouting inflamed punctum and discharge. Because topical antibiotics cannot eradicate organisms sequestered within the concretions, mechanical removal is generally required for cure.
additionalDifferentials: Herpetic or other viral lid disease
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the pouting punctum and expressible concretions
Microbiological examination and culture of expressed material
Assessment of the lacrimal drainage system
Imaging only if a tumour or extensive disease is suspected
Examination for concretions at the time of any procedure
redFlags: A mass or atypical lesion suggesting canalicular tumour
Spread to dacryocystitis or surrounding tissues
Failure to resolve after concretion removal
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent once the concretions are removed, though cases treated with antibiotics alone tend to recur until the sequestered material is cleared.
pitfalls: Treating it repeatedly as conjunctivitis and missing the diagnosis
Relying on topical antibiotics without removing concretions
Not sending expressed material for microbiology
references: Oculoplastic and lacrimal surgery references (standard reference)
management: Achieve cure by mechanically removing the causative concretions, typically through canaliculotomy and curettage
Express the canaliculus and dilate the punctum to evacuate dacryoliths
Use topical antibiotic drops or canalicular irrigation as an adjunct directed against Actinomyces and other cultured organisms
Apply warm compresses and canalicular massage to aid drainage
Send expressed material for microscopy and culture to guide adjunctive therapy
Follow up to confirm resolution, recognising that antibiotic treatment alone recurs until the sequestered material is cleared
